CausalChain: GEMIN5 upregulation -> Aberrant splicing of DNA repair regulators (RAD51, MRE11) -> Production of non-canonical isoforms favoring error-prone repair (BIR) -> Increased genomic instability -> Enhanced metastasis/angiogenesis -> Poorer liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, elevated levels of GEMIN5 directly modulate the splicing of key DNA repair genes, specifically RAD51 and MRE11, leading to the production of alternative isoforms that impair canonical double-strand break repair. Instead of promoting high-fidelity homologous recombination, these isoform shifts favor error-prone break-induced replication. This repair pathway switch results in accelerated genomic instability, which in turn drives the metastatic and angiogenic processes characteristic of aggressive liver cancers. To dissect this mechanism, we will employ CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing to alter GEMIN5 expression, coupled with high-throughput RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, and quantitative proteomic analyses, as well as splicing reporter assays and single-cell transcriptomics. These contemporary technologies will enable us to capture both the direct interactions of GEMIN5 with repair regulator pre-mRNAs and the downstream functional effects on DNA repair fidelity, thereby establishing GEMIN5-mediated splicing alteration as a novel therapeutic target in liver cancer.
Abstract: We propose that in liver neoplasms, overexpression of the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 leads to a distinct pattern of alternative splicing in key double-strand break (DSB) repair regulators, notably RAD51 and MRE11. This alteration produces non-canonical isoforms that shift the balance from high-fidelity homologous recombination repair toward an error-prone mechanism, namely break-induced replication (BIR). The consequent genomic instability fosters tumor microenvironment changes that facilitate metastasis and angiogenesis, thereby contributing to a poorer clinical prognosis. Our approach integrates CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated GEMIN5 modulation, high-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP‐seq) for detailed splicing and RNA−protein interaction analyses, as well as advanced proteomic profiling and single-cell transcriptomics. This multimodal strategy is designed to offer unprecedented resolution in mapping the dynamic interplay between splicing regulation and DNA repair alterations in liver cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that GEMIN5 overexpression alters the splicing and regulation of RAD51 and MRE11, shifting repair from high-fidelity mechanisms to error-prone break-induced replication, leading to genomic instability and aggressive tumor behavior. In the revised hypothesis, we explicitly delineate the causative splicing events by proposing that GEMIN5 generates non-canonical isoforms of RAD51 and MRE11 which favor a switch to error-prone BIR. We also integrate additional modern techniques such as high-throughput RNA sequencing, single-cell transcriptomics, and splicing reporter assays to dynamically capture the process, thereby enhancing the practical implementability of the study. Each critical step of the original causal chain is preserved but now benefits from a more detailed mechanistic explanation and a robust experimental strategy that leverages contemporary technologies.
